sections.narration:
Welcome. Today we are exploring Loosen Your Speaking Rules. You want to speak, but there are conditions: no pauses, no repeated words, no visible nerves, no asking for time. Even an ordinary answer has become a narrow corridor.

In this session, we will recognise a speaking rule, keep the value beneath it, and try a flexible permission. I will explain the idea, show a visual example, and invite you to try it in a small experience of your own. You can ask me a question or switch to reading at any point. We will finish by choosing what, if anything, you want to take into a real conversation.

sections.narration: A speaking rule is a condition you believe must be met for communication to be acceptable. Some rules serve the message, such as checking that you were understood. Others may be so strict that they make participation difficult. We will examine one rule and try a more flexible version, while keeping the value underneath it.

sections.narration:
You want to speak, but there are conditions: no pauses, no repeated words, no visible nerves, no asking for time. Even an ordinary answer has become a narrow corridor.

If your rule is never pause, the value may be respecting another person’s time. Respect can also mean taking a short moment to give a useful answer. If the rule is never ask for clarification, the value may be competence. Competence can include knowing when you need more information. Flexibility offers more ways to honour the value.

Record only when you choose. Afterwards save one observation rather than decide what this says about you as a person.

sections.narration: Do not turn permission into another rule. You do not have to pause in every sentence just because pauses are allowed. Choose what serves this moment. A changed, unchanged or uncertain experience is information, not a grade. You do not have to report relief for this attempt to count as exploration.

sections.narration: Use your flexible alternative in one low-pressure exchange. Notice whether the original value was actually lost. During focused practice, you can deliberately explore this one tool. In an everyday conversation, give most of your attention to the message and the other person. A familiar support can be available if it helps; you do not have to monitor the tool throughout the exchange.
